title: Karmic tail 15-5-8 in the destiny matrix: betrayal in the family, a blessing turned inside out and a chain of flowers

seo.title: Karmic Tail 15-5-8 “Betrayal in the Family” in the Destiny Matrix
seo.description: 15-5-8 is the tail where a rule covers a craving. A ten-second date check, why Waite’s Devil is the Hierophant inside out, and Strength or Justice at the root.

short: 15-5-8 is the karmic tail that popular destiny matrix readings call “Betrayal in the Family” (less often, “Betrayal and Passions in the Family”). Its script is a life with a right side and a wrong side. On the right side are rules, vows, family, “the proper way”. On the wrong side is a pull that won’t let go: a passion, a person, money, gambling, a habit, the forbidden. The rule covers the pull, the pull wears away the rule, and betrayal begins where the wrong side lives behind the back of the right one. The Devil (15) opens the circle: a desire that becomes a chain. The Hierophant (5) holds it: a rule that either hides the chain or turns into one itself. At the root stands Strength (8): a woman leading a lion on a chain of flowers — the ability to hold your own passion from within, without a ban and without a secret. (Many calculators call the eight Justice — more on that below; the task stays the same.) So the main question of the tail is not “how do I resist temptation” or “how do I not betray”, but how to make the right side and the wrong side one life. And everyone with 15-5-8 also has a hidden fourth card — the Chariot in the centre of the matrix.

sections.h2: Do you have the 15-5-8 tail: a ten-second check
paragraphs: The tail depends entirely on one number — the sum of the first three arcana of the matrix. So you can find 15-5-8 without a calculator.

ol: **Day arcanum** — your day of birth. If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 25 → 7, 31 → 4.
**Year arcanum** — the sum of the digits of the year. If the result is greater than 22, add the digits again: 1988 → 26 → 8, while 1990 → 19.

paragraphs: Add up the three numbers. If you get **26, 35, 44 or 53**, you have 15-5-8. Most often it is 26 or 35: they account for 85% of cases. The sum 53 is rare, about one case in eighty.

ul: 02.04.2000: 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 → not this one. That is 6-14-8: the same eight at the root, but a different entry and a different tail.

paragraphs: Why this works. The digits of the sums 26, 35, 44 and 53 add up to 8, so the bottom corner of the chart is D = 8. The centre E is the same sum plus D: 26 + 8 = 34 → 7. The other sums also give 7: 43, 52 and 61 reduce to seven. The entry of the tail is M = D + E = 8 + 7 = 15, the middle N = D + M = 8 + 15 = 23 → 5. The sum 8 also puts an eight in the corner, but its centre is 16, and the tail comes out as 6-14-8. There are no other routes to 15-5-8 — this was checked by going through every day from 1900 to 2100.
Three tails begin with the Devil, and one more shares its root with 15-5-8. They are often confused:
The same arithmetic leads to facts you rarely come across:

ul: **It is one of the most common tails.** Among birth dates from 1940 to 2012, 15-5-8 comes up for roughly one in eleven (8.8%) — 2nd place out of 26 possible, after 15-20-5. And the three tails that begin with the Devil together go to more than one person in five (22%).

**It is getting rarer.** Among people born in the 1950s it is one in 10, in the 1990s one in 12, and from 2000 to 2025 one in 15, 3rd place. The reason is arithmetic: you need a sum of 26 or more. Years of the 20th century have a large arcanum (1984 → 22), and the day and month don’t have much to make up. The year 2000 has arcanum 2, and only late days of late months make it to 26.

**It never disappears in any year.** From 1900 to 2100, every year has between 13 and 42 such dates. The most are in years with arcanum 21 or 22: 1938, 1947, 1948, 1956, 1965, 1974, 1983, 1984 and 1992 have 42 dates each. The fewest are in 2000: 13 dates, and all of them work the same way. The day and month add up to 24 or 33: 22.02, 21.03, 20.04 and so on up to 12.12 and 21.12.
**It likes the end of the year.** The month number is part of the sum, so there are one and a half times as many December dates with this tail as January ones.

**8-5-15 is the same tail.** If you see 8, 5 and 15 on the bottom ray of your chart, you are reading the same tail from the outer corner towards the centre. No tail in this scheme begins with an eight: the inner point M is always a multiple of three (3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21). The roles don’t change: the Devil is the entry, Strength is the root.

sections.h2: Why 15-5-8 is called “Betrayal in the Family”
paragraphs: Popular readings explain the name with a past-life legend. The soul supposedly cheated within a family or lived with an addiction that hurt the people close to it. And in the present life the person seems perfectly respectable but every now and then slides back into the old ways: changes partners, or ends up next to someone who is addicted and drags them down. This cannot be checked; the numbers say nothing about past events. But as a metaphor the legend is accurate. “Seems respectable” and “slides back into the old ways” are exactly the right side and the wrong side, the two sides of one life.

The word “family” in the name rests on the middle card. Waite’s divinatory meanings for the Hierophant begin with the words “marriage, alliance” — and right after them come “captivity, servitude”. In old decks this card was called the Pope: the one who seals vows. Waite’s four words hold the whole mechanism of the tail: a union that quietly becomes captivity.

The word “betrayal” is explained by the Waite deck itself. Put the fifth and fifteenth cards side by side — they share one composition. A figure at the top raises its right hand, with two figures below. Two ministers kneel before the Hierophant; two chained figures stand at the foot of the Devil. Waite says this outright: the Devil’s raised hand is “the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card”. He also compares the chained pair with the figures “of the fifth card” (scholars argue whether this is a misprint for the sixth — the Lovers). The Devil in this deck is the Hierophant turned inside out. And betrayal is exactly a vow turned inside out: the same words, the same gesture, the opposite meaning.

Benebell Wen has one more thread that ties these cards together. She retells two versions of where the images came from, and both lead to the case of the Knights Templar. The dark reading of the Hierophant is linked to Pope Clement V, under whom the order was crushed. The look of the Devil is linked to Baphomet, the idol the Templars were accused of worshipping. The history itself is well known. In October 1307, on the orders of King Philip IV, the Templars were arrested all over France. In August 1308 cardinals sent by the pope granted the order’s leaders absolution. There was no publicity: the parchment with this decision was found in the Vatican archives only in 2001. In 1312 the same pope dissolved the order, and two years later the grand master Jacques de Molay was burned in Paris. An order that had served the Church for almost two centuries was forgiven in private and condemned in full view of everyone.

More than five centuries later, Éliphas Lévi drew Baphomet with a goat’s head — in a book called “Dogma and Ritual of High Magic”. According to Waite, it was Lévi’s influence that “changed the face” of the Devil card. Wen even compares the Chariot, which stands in the centre for everyone with this tail, to the Templars returning from the East. All these are versions, not the proven origin of the cards, and the destiny matrix did not take its name from here. But you could hardly invent a better story in which a rule, a secret and a charge of idolatry wove together into one betrayal.

And one last thing. In the numbering most matrix calculators use, the eight is Justice: scales and a sword. A vow, a temptation and scales — that is how the three cards make up a story of infidelity and reckoning. The two names of the eight get their own section below.

sections.h2: Chain, keys and flowers: how the circle works
paragraphs: In the Waite deck, each card of this tail has its own bonds. The Devil has an iron chain around the neck. The Hierophant has crossed keys at his feet: in church symbolism, the power “to bind and to loose”. Strength has a chain of flowers on which the woman leads the lion. The tail describes how a person moves from the first bonds to the second and why they need the third.

**1. Entry: the Devil — a pull that becomes a chain.** Waite describes on the card “the chain and fatality of the material life”: two figures are chained to an altar, they have animal tails but human faces — the mind has not gone anywhere. Wen names the essence of the card precisely: bondage to the material and the superficial, a preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification. And she sets it apart from the Lovers in one phrase: the sixth card is about “one choice”, the fifteenth is about “being led astray”. In 15-5-8 everything starts with desire, and the object can be anything: a person, a passion, money, status, gambling, sweets, the phone at two in the morning, other people’s admiration. The Devil, Wen stresses, is not a literal demon but human selfishness and indulging in it. And an important detail: in Waite’s divinatory list the Devil has “extraordinary efforts, force”. There is a lot of power in this pull. The trouble is not that there is too little of it, but that it went the wrong way.
**2. Mechanism: the Hierophant — the rule that holds.** Next the fifth card comes into play, and it works in two ways.

The first way is **cover**. The rule gives the pull a decent look and a place in the schedule: “we’re a normal family”, “everyone lives like this”, “that’s how men are”, “Fridays are allowed”. Wen writes that the Hierophant is a card of conformity, and to conform you have to suppress what sets you apart from others. That is why it is also a card of concealment. Wen writes that the card can suggest “a good intention to protect, but a negative result from those good intentions”: the truth is hidden from loved ones for their own good — “we don’t tell Mum”, “the children don’t need to know”. No one, she adds, should assume they know better than another and shield them from the truth.

The second way is **the rule becomes the chain itself**. Wen directly links the Devil with “dogma, despotism and enslavement”. Waite sees the same danger in the Hierophant: the pontiff may forget that he only represents something greater and act as if he himself contained everything his sign stands for. The form outlives the content. A marriage rests on “that’s the proper way”, a job on “stability”, faith on fear. In both cases the rule does not free you from the chain. It gives it a name, a schedule and a place in the house.

This mechanism has a flip side well known to psychologists. The addiction researcher Alan Marlatt described the “abstinence violation effect”: if a person has set themselves an absolute “never”, the first slip often turns into a full relapse — since the rule is broken anyway, there is no point holding on. The Hierophant writes “never”; the Devil waits for the first exception.

**3. Root: Strength — a lion on a chain of flowers.** On Waite’s card a woman is closing a lion’s jaws. Her “beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion”, and he follows her on a chain of flowers. The lion, for Waite, signifies the passions, and Strength herself is “the higher nature in its liberation”. He explains the chain of flowers as “the sweet yoke and the light burden of Divine Law, when it has been taken into the heart of hearts”. Wen adds a detail that sounds almost literal for this tail. The lion on the card reminds her of a line from the First Epistle of Peter: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” The Devil of the entry comes back at the root as a lion. And it is tamed, according to Wen, through kindness and compassion, not brute force: “The meek lamb will prevail over the open-mouthed lion.”

The root task of the tail is not to kill the passion or lock it up behind rules, but to keep it beside you openly and gently. The lion stays a lion, the chain stays a chain. What changes is the material: a law that pressed from outside with keys becomes a law taken into the heart.

**4. Repeat.** Until the root is lived through, the circle repeats. A pull, a ban — “never again”, a secret exception, a lapse, shame — and an even stricter ban. With each turn the rule gets harsher and the secret deeper. In the family version the circle is the same, only spread over several people: one has the pull, the family has the rule “don’t wash your dirty linen in public”, and all of them together have the secret. When the secret one day comes out, the very word from the tail’s name appears.

paragraphs: Many people with 15-5-8 recognise all three modes in themselves — in different years, and sometimes within one week. A strict period, a lapse, shame and secrecy, then strictness again — this time towards others.

The Guard is the least visible mode. The person “breaks” nothing themselves, but their life is organised around someone else’s Devil: a partner who drinks, a son with debts, a parent who gambles. The popular legend about “a partner with an addiction” is exactly about this mode. The Hierophant here is aimed at the other person: rules, checks, cover in front of relatives and at work. In Wen’s discussion of the Hierophant there is a sentence that fits here most precisely: “We are not the keeper of others.”

The Free Fall is the opposite extreme: the rules are declared hypocrisy, and since everyone lies, anything goes. But this is the same tail too. The Free Fall is not free of the Hierophant — it argues with him, which means it still obeys him, only with a minus sign.

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: everyone with 15-5-8 has the Chariot in the centre
paragraphs: Everyone who has the 15-5-8 tail has 7, the Chariot, in the centre of the matrix. This is not a coincidence but arithmetic: the centre always equals 7, and the method derives the entry of the tail from it. So the Devil of this tail is literally made of two cards: 15 = 8 + 7, Strength plus the Chariot. Wen puts these cards side by side and tells them apart with one pair of phrases: the Chariot is the strength to master the world, Strength is the strength to master the self. What follows is our reading, not a rule of the method: the pull of 15-5-8 is not weakness but a great deal of strength that has no channel of its own. Power over the world and power over yourself, added together and finding no work to do, become the Devil.

In the method, the centre of the chart is the comfort zone, the state a person returns to when nothing is demanded of them. For 15-5-8 this leads to a familiar picture: here people are used to fighting their pull. Quit by willpower, keep yourself on a tight rein, plan life point by point, take control of yourself — and of everyone around while you’re at it. The Chariot really does know how to win. Waite says of the charioteer: “He has led captivity captive.” But he immediately adds that the planes of his conquest are external “and not within himself”, and that the liberation he brings about may leave him in bondage. Wen notes that the Chariot person likes to appear in control but tends to run from problems — or attack them so aggressively as to avoid a truly mature confrontation. And she asks a question that should make anyone with 15-5-8 flinch: who exactly is in control — the sphinxes or the charioteer?

That is why the key to the tail is the path from the centre to the root, from the Chariot to Strength. The charioteer holds the sphinxes by will; the woman holds the lion by closeness. Will works while there is strength left; closeness holds even when there is none. This tail knows how to defeat its pull like an outside enemy. What it needs is something else: to stop fighting it and learn to lead it on a chain of flowers.

sections.h2: Strength or Justice: why the eight has two names
paragraphs: If you calculated your matrix with another calculator, you most likely saw not Strength but Justice at the root of this tail. There is no mistake here — there are two numberings. In the old Marseille order of the cards Justice is eighth and Strength eleventh, and most destiny matrix calculators and readings keep this order. Waite swapped them and in his 1910 book explained it with one phrase: “for reasons which satisfy myself”. For the reader, he added, the change signifies nothing. In this article the eight is read by the Waite deck — as Strength.

If your root is Justice, read it like this. Waite sees in this card “the moral principle which deals unto every man according to his works”, and in the divinatory list, “equity, rightness, probity”. Wen sees human-made justice: a decision made fairly and impartially, and the consequences of our decisions and actions. Popular readings call this the boomerang law. In the 15-5-8 tail such an eight means honest scales between the right side and the wrong side. On one pan, the vows; on the other, what actually pulls you; and you decide in the light. A promise is either kept or openly reconsidered, but never broken in silence. Hence the popular reading of the tail as a story of infidelity and reckoning.

The two readings of the root do not argue but complete each other. Strength answers how to hold your lion. Justice answers how to hold your word. In this tail one doesn’t work without the other: **a lion nobody talks about can’t be held, and a word given on top of an untamed lion won’t hold.** Curiously, the neighbouring tail 15-8-11 has both cards at once: Strength in the middle and Justice at the root (in the Marseille numbering, the other way round).

sections.h2: The tail in the mirror: where else 15, 5 and 8 stand in your chart
paragraphs: The 15-5-8 trio appears in the matrix not only on the bottom ray. Going through all dates from 1900 to 2100 finds two more places where it stands in full, and one where everyone with the tail has its Devil.

**The relationship line always starts with the Devil.** Point M, the entry of the tail, is shared in the method with the relationship line M–R1–R. So for everyone with 15-5-8 the relationship programme also opens with the fifteenth arcanum. And for people born in years with arcanum 4, 13 or 22 — 1930, 1939, 1948, 1957, 1966, 1975, 1984, 1993, 2002, 2011, 2020 — the relationship line repeats the tail in full: 15-5-8. That is roughly one holder of the tail in nine. For them “in the family” from the name sounds literal: one and the same script is written into the chart twice — as an old circle and as a way of building closeness.

**For those born in August, the tail is reflected in a mirror.** The month number stands on the top ray of the chart, at the start of the talent line. For holders of 15-5-8 born in August there is an eight there, and the talent line comes out as 8-5-15. These are the same three cards, standing the same way as below: the eight at the outer corner, the Devil next to the centre. The bottom ray is reflected in the top one, as in water. What follows is our reading: for these people the trap and the gift are made of the same material. What has to be tamed in the tail becomes, in the talent, an ability to understand other people’s lions — temptation, money, passion and addiction — from the inside, without ending up on the chain.

**The Devil always stands in Svadhisthana.** In the matrix’s chakra table, point M is Svadhisthana’s Energy, the chakra of joy, children and creativity. Everyone with the 15-5-8 tail has the Devil there, and in Manipura the Chariot twice, with Temperance in the Emotions column. Our reading: the pull of this tail grows out of joy. When pleasure has no legitimate place on the right side of life, it goes to the wrong side. And Temperance in Manipura hints at the same thing as Strength, only in other words: measure instead of a ban.
The scenes below are made-up examples, not a description of every person with this tail.
The tail is most often recognised by three storylines.

**A double life.** The union rests on duty: the children, the mortgage, “what will the family say”, “we were married in church”. But life goes somewhere else — into an affair, a secret account, a hobby that eats up every evening, a second phone. On the outside everything is respectable, and the person often believes nothing is happening: “this doesn’t count”, “I’m not going anywhere”. This is the Hierophant covering the Devil — the Facade from the table above.

**Next to someone else’s chain.** The script from the popular legend: a partner drinks, gambles or runs up debts, and the person with 15-5-8 becomes their warden and their lawyer at the same time. They hide things, check up, cover for them in front of relatives, set rules — and live for years by the schedule of someone else’s pull. Imagine a woman who for fifteen years calls her husband’s boss to say he is “a bit under the weather”. Nobody would call her a traitor. But in this story the secret betrays everyone: the children, who see everything, and herself — her own life is on pause.

**Passion under the name of duty.** The third storyline is jealousy and power. “Since you’re my wife, you’re mine”, “since we’re a family, you have to”. The Devil puts on the Hierophant’s robes: he calls possession marriage, and control care. It is no accident that Wen links the Devil with despotism. These are the “passions in the family” from the second version of the name.

The strong version in all three storylines is the same — an honest agreement. Say out loud what pulls you. Reconsider what no longer holds. Leave the other person the right to their own lion. This tail is not about faithfulness being impossible. It is about the fact that **faithfulness holds only on what has been chosen, not on what has been hidden.**

The Devil is the card of the material, the Hierophant the card of the institution. At work, the two locked together look like “golden handcuffs”. A person spends years at a company they don’t respect: the salary, the status, “everyone in our family worked at one place until they retired”. Or the rules of the system start covering what shouldn’t be covered: “everyone does it”, “that’s how it works in this industry”, “it’s not stealing, it’s a bonus”. Corporate dogma is the most convenient costume for the Devil. A separate form of betrayal is aimed at partners: poaching clients, quietly starting your own business on company time, breaking an agreement and saying nothing. It usually begins not with an act but with rules changed in silence.

The strength here is real. People with 15-5-8 understand money, power and temptation from the inside and are not afraid to talk about them. They manage what moralists can’t: discussing risk, profit and temptation without shame and without self-deception. In the worked-through version they make good mentors, negotiators, financiers, lawyers and managers — people you can trust with the keys precisely because they know how easy it is to turn them the wrong way.

Family rules and family secrets are the main material of this tail. “We don’t talk about that”: that Grandad drank, that Dad had a second family, that money appeared in the house in strange ways. Double standards: “do as I say, not as I do”. A child learns the main rule of such a home early — rules exist for the shop window. Popular readings often say that people with 15-5-8 grew up next to someone’s addiction or infidelity. The numbers know nothing about your childhood. But if this rings true, the link is plain to see: someone who kept another person’s secret as a child easily keeps their own as an adult.

A parent with this tail should take a close look at two things. Whether their parenting rests on bans they don’t keep themselves. And whether they hide the truth from their children “for their own good” — Wen writes that such protection hurts more than it helps. The honest question here is: what can be said out loud in our family — and what has the child already guessed?

sections.h2: Faithfulness or a chain: how to tell them apart
paragraphs: **Faithfulness or a chain:**

ul: Would you choose this again today if nobody were watching and nobody would say a word?
What holds you: love, fear or “that’s the proper way”? If the rule were cancelled tomorrow, would you stay?
Can you name the price of your choice — and are you willing to pay it?
Can you explain the rule in your own words — why it exists?
Who set it: you now, you ten years ago, or someone before you?
Is it for everyone — or only for others, with secret exceptions for yourself?

paragraphs: **Strength or a bridle:**

ul: After you “pulled yourself together”, did you feel calmer or just heavier?
Is the pull weakening — or waiting for night, a holiday, the first exception?
Could you tell one person about it without shame and without excuses?

paragraphs: **A secret or something private:**

ul: Something private concerns only you. A secret would change the decisions of the person you have an agreement with.
Something private needs no lies. A secret has to be guarded.
If someone close to you found out, would they say “that’s your business” — or “why didn’t you tell me”?

sections.h2: What to do with the 15-5-8 tail: seven practices
paragraphs: These are the author’s exercises, drawn from the logic of the trio — not a ritual and not a promise of results.

ol: **Three chains.** Write down everything that holds you: people, work, habits, rules. Next to each item, put one of three marks. Iron — I can’t stop, though I want to. Keys — I hold on because it’s “the proper way” and because of “what people will say”. Flowers — I choose this today too, knowing the price. The task is not to break everything off. Keep the flowers, reconsider the keys, speak about the iron out loud.

**Name the lion in front of a witness.** The Devil’s main ally in this tail is secrecy, and the Hierophant gladly supplies it. Tell one trusted person about your pull — without excuses and without vows of “never again”. What has been said out loud loses half its power. In Waite, the chained figures have human faces: your mind stays with you.

**Your own charter.** Write down the rules your family lives by: “we don’t get divorced”, “we don’t talk about bad things”, “money spoils people”, “put up with it, you’re a mother”, “a man has to”. Next to each, write who set it, why, and whether it works now. Keep the ones you can explain in your own words. A rule you have understood and accepted is a chain of flowers. A rule you obey out of fear is keys in someone else’s hand.

**Feed the lion, don’t just restrain it.** Behind every pull there is a legitimate need: rest, excitement, warmth, recognition, oblivion, the right to pleasure. Ask yourself what the pull really gives you, and find a way to give the lion part of that openly. A lion that has only a muzzle will wait for the night. It is no accident that Wen writes that Strength’s lion is tamed by kindness, not brute force.

**A plan for a lapse.** Before you set yourself a rule, decide what you will do if you break it. One lapse is a lapse, not a reason to give up: the next day, back to the plan, without punishing yourself. A rule without a plan for a lapse is a ready-made turn of that very circle.

**Reconsider, don’t break.** If an agreement no longer works — in a couple, in the family, at work — say so before you break it. “I feel cramped in our agreement, let’s revisit it” is a harder sentence than any secret, but it is the only one that leads out of the circle. Betrayal begins not with an act but with rules changed in silence. This is the practice of the eight under both its names — Strength and Justice.

**Separate someone else’s lion.** If the pull lives not in you but in someone close to you, you cannot tame their lion for them. Your area is your own boundaries, your own truth, your own life. When it comes to addiction — to drink, drugs, gambling or debt — this is not karma but a reason to turn to addiction specialists. For relatives there are mutual support groups, such as Al-Anon.

sections.h2: The strength of 15-5-8: one who leads the lion on flowers
paragraphs: In its worked-through version this tail gives a rare combination. The person knows passion from the inside (the Devil), can keep form — a word, a vow, the rules of a business (the Hierophant) — and is not afraid of their own power (Strength). You can trust them with money, power and other people’s secrets: not because they are never tempted, but because they know how temptation pulls and they say so out loud. People come to them for advice with their most shameful stories, because they don’t moralise. This is the Hierophant at his best: a mentor without hypocrisy.

Waite writes of the Devil that he is blind to “the liberty of service”. The worked-through tail has it: it serves its vows not out of fear but by choice. In Waite’s divinatory list for Strength stand “power, energy, action, courage, magnanimity” — the same might as the Devil’s, only turned the right side out.

Waite ends his description of the Devil with a promise: the one exalted above the chained figures “is not to be their master for ever”. In his deck one and the same chain appears twice — iron on the fifteenth card and of flowers on the eighth. The 15-5-8 tail is the path from one to the other. The chain stays. The material changes.

sections.h2: What this article is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M; every sum greater than 22 is reduced by adding its digits. All numerical facts in the article — the sums 26, 35, 44 and 53, the constant centre 7, frequencies by year, month and generation, matches with the relationship and talent lines, constant numbers in the chakras — were obtained by going through all dates from 1900 to 2100. Shares were calculated over dates from 1940 to 2012, by decade and over dates from 2000 to 2025.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922) and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotes are given in the original English. Card numbering follows Waite: VIII is Strength, XI is Justice. The Bible line is quoted as Wen gives it.

**The history of the Templars** — well-known facts of the 1307–1314 trial and the Chinon parchment. The links of the Hierophant with Pope Clement V, the Devil with Baphomet and the Chariot with the Templars are versions that Wen cites, not the proven origin of the cards.
**The abstinence violation effect** — a concept from the work of the psychologist Alan Marlatt on how people return to addictive behaviour after a first slip.

**The name “Betrayal in the Family” and the past-life legend** come from popular destiny matrix readings. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the matrix or karmic tails: putting the three cards together into a script, the reading of the centre, the mirror matches and the chakras are the author’s interpretation.

This is an esoteric model for self-reflection, not a forecast and not a substitute for professional help. If there is violence, threats or addiction in the family, it is not about the tail and not about you: what is needed here is real help, not work with numbers.

faq.q: What happened in a past life of someone with the 15-5-8 tail?
faq.a: Popular readings speak of infidelity in a family or of an addiction that hurt loved ones. Less often, of an abuse of power, or of the person becoming a victim of someone else’s passion. This is a legend of the tradition: neither numbers nor cards establish events of past lives. It is more useful to read it as a description of what is already visible now: a habit of hiding a pull behind rules, or of living next to someone else’s pull and guarding its secret.

faq.q: Does 15-5-8 mean that I will cheat, be cheated on or become addicted?
faq.a: No. The tail predicts neither infidelity nor addiction, nor any events at all. It describes a way of dealing with desire and rules that may repeat. Among Waite’s meanings for the Devil there is an important caveat: it is “that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil”. Wen adds that this card does not necessarily mean the person is entirely to blame. The name is scarier than the script: its weight lies in going unnoticed, not in fate.

faq.q: Why is 8 Strength in one calculator and Justice in another?
faq.a: These are two numberings of the deck. In the old Marseille order and in most matrix calculators the eighth card is Justice and the eleventh Strength. Waite swapped them, and in his deck the eighth is Strength. The tail doesn’t change because of this: the numbers are the same, only the name of the root changes. How to read the root in both numberings is covered in the section “Strength or Justice” above.

Yes, if 8, 5 and 15 stand on the bottom ray of your chart: you have simply read the tail from the outer corner towards the centre. In the calculation it is written from the inner point M to the corner D, and M is always a multiple of three, so there is no tail that begins with an eight. The roles don’t change: 15 is the entry, 8 the root. But 8-5-15 also occurs on the top ray — in the talent line of holders of the tail born in August. There it is no longer a tail but its mirror reflection.

faq.q: Are the 15-5-8 tail and the “15-5-8 programme” in relationships the same thing?
faq.a: A karmic tail is only the trio on the bottom ray, between the centre and the bottom corner of the chart. The same numbers occur on the relationship line M–R1–R: for holders of the tail born in years with arcanum 4, 13 or 22, and sometimes for people without this tail. There the trio describes not an old script but how you build closeness: entering through passion, union through a vow, the outcome through Strength. If you have it in both places, the practices in this article apply to both.

All three tails begin with the Devil — they share an entry, the pull. What differs is what holds the circle and what it teaches. In 15-20-5 (“the Rebel” in popular lists) Judgement is in the middle and the Hierophant stands at the root: the rule there is a task to be found after the rebellion. In 15-5-8 the Hierophant is in the middle: the rule here is a trap that has to be rebuilt. In 15-8-11 (“Physical Aggression” in popular lists) Strength holds the pull, and Justice is at the root if you count by Waite: there the question is where to direct the power. The three tails also have different centres: the Wheel of Fortune, the Chariot and the Emperor.

faq.q: Is 15-5-8 different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in the calculation, and the meaning of the tail does not depend on it. Popular readings like to split it into “a woman who uses seduction” and “a man who fights his instincts”, but these are stereotypes, not arithmetic. Anyone can be the Facade, the Guard or the Free Fall — and most often it is one and the same person in different years.

faq.q: Who is a person with the 15-5-8 tail compatible with?
faq.a: You come across advice to choose a partner by numbers: “good with fives and eights, dangerous with fifteens and sixteens”. Neither the method of calculation nor the meanings of the cards give any such rules. The tail describes your own script, not whom you can or cannot play it out with. A more reliable question is this: can you talk with this person about what pulls you, and revisit agreements out loud?

The numbers in the matrix don’t change — what changes is how the script plays out. Signs of a worked-through tail: the pull can be named out loud; the rules are chosen and explained in your own words; agreements are reconsidered, not broken; a lapse doesn’t become a reason to give up; you don’t keep someone else’s lion on your own chain. And most of all: the right side and the wrong side of your life no longer argue with each other.

faq.q: What should I do if my child has 15-5-8?
faq.a: Give them what this tail lacks: rules with explanations and truth without secrets. Explain why a rule exists, don’t just demand. Don’t hide family difficulties from them “for their own good”, but talk about them in simple words, suited to their age. Don’t shame them for their desires, but teach them to name those desires and find a place for them. And keep your own rules yourself: a child with this tail is especially quick to notice where adults live double lives. There are quite a few such children: among those born since 2000, roughly one in fifteen gets 15-5-8.

report: “Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude” — so begins Waite’s list of divinatory meanings for the Hierophant, the fifth card. Alliance and captivity sit side by side, a comma apart. Those four words hold the whole 15-5-8 tail: a union that quietly turns into captivity.

Popular readings call the tail “Betrayal in the Family”. In the legend, the soul in a past life was unfaithful or lived with an addiction that hurt its loved ones; now the person seems respectable but now and then slides back into the old ways. This cannot be checked: numbers say nothing about the past. But as a metaphor the legend is exact. “Seems respectable” and “slides back into the old ways” are the right and wrong sides of one life. On the right side: vows, family, “the proper way”. On the wrong side: a pull that won’t let go.

The Waite deck itself explains the word “betrayal”. Its fifth and fifteenth cards share one design: a figure above raises its right hand, two figures below — kneeling ministers before the Hierophant, chained ones at the Devil’s feet. Waite is explicit: the Devil’s raised hand is “the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant”. **In this deck the Devil is the Hierophant turned inside out.** And betrayal is a vow turned inside out: same words, same gesture, opposite meaning.

report.h3: The Hierophant writes “never”; the Devil waits for the exception

report: In the Waite deck each card of the tail has its own bonds: the Devil, an iron chain around the neck; the Hierophant, crossed keys — in church symbolism, the power “to bind and to loose”; Strength, a chain of flowers on which a woman leads a lion.

The entry is the Devil: a pull that becomes a chain. Wen separates it from the Lovers in a phrase: the sixth card is about “one choice”, the fifteenth about “being led astray”. The object can be anything: a person, money, gambling, the phone at two in the morning.

The Hierophant holds the circle in two ways. The first is cover: “we’re a normal family”, “everyone lives like this”, “Fridays are allowed”. Wen writes that the card can suggest “a good intention to protect, but a negative result”: hiding the truth from loved ones for their own good, “we don’t tell Mum”. In the second, the rule becomes the chain: a marriage rests on “that’s the proper way”, a job on “stability”, faith on fear. **The rule frees no one from the chain — it gives it a name, a schedule and a place in the house.**

Psychologist Alan Marlatt described the “abstinence violation effect”: after an absolute “never”, the first slip often becomes a full relapse — the rule is broken anyway, so why hold on. So the circle turns: a pull, “never again”, a secret exception, a lapse, shame — and a stricter ban. Each turn buries the secret deeper. When it comes out, the word in the tail’s name appears.

report.h3: A secret betrays its keeper too

report: The tail has three modes, and many recognise all three — in different years, sometimes in one week. The Facade keeps up appearances while life drains into an affair, a secret account, a second phone: “this doesn’t count”. The Free Fall declares the rules hypocrisy, but by arguing with the Hierophant it still obeys him — only with a minus sign.

The least visible mode is the Guard. The person breaks nothing, yet lives around someone else’s Devil: a partner who drinks, a son with debts. A made-up scene: for fifteen years a woman calls her husband’s boss to say he is “a bit under the weather”. Nobody would call her a traitor. But here the secret betrays everyone: the children, who see everything, and her, whose own life is on pause. As Wen puts it: “We are not the keeper of others.”

report.h3: The Chariot conquers everything except the charioteer

report: Everyone with 15-5-8 has 7, the Chariot, in the centre of the matrix, and the tail’s Devil is made of two cards: 15 = 8 + 7, Strength plus the Chariot. Wen tells them apart in two phrases: the Chariot is the strength to master the world, Strength the strength to master the self. Our reading from here: the pull of 15-5-8 is not weakness but much strength with no channel of its own. No wonder Waite lists “extraordinary efforts, force” among the Devil’s meanings.

The centre of the chart is the comfort zone, so the habit here is to fight the pull: quit by willpower, keep a tight rein, and control everyone else too. Waite says of the charioteer: “He has led captivity captive.” But his conquests are external, “and not within himself”.

The tail’s root is Strength. On Waite’s card a woman closes a lion’s jaws and leads him on a chain of flowers. Waite reads that chain as “the sweet yoke and the light burden of Divine Law, when it has been taken into the heart of hearts”. The lion reminds Wen of a line from 1 Peter: “the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour”. The Devil of the entry returns at the root as a lion. It is tamed, Wen says, through kindness and compassion: “The meek lamb will prevail over the open-mouthed lion.” The charioteer rules by will; the woman, by closeness. **Will works while there is strength left; closeness holds even when there is none.**

report.h3: Betrayal begins with rules changed in silence

report: The way out is not a vow but an honest inventory:

ul: Sort everything that has a hold — people, work, habits, rules — into three chains. Iron: I can’t stop, though I want to. Keys: I hold on because it’s “the proper way”. Flowers: I still choose this today, knowing the price. Keep the flowers, rethink the keys, say the iron out loud.
Name the pull to one trusted person — without excuses or vows of “never again”. The Devil’s main ally here is secrecy.
Decide in advance what to do after breaking a rule: one lapse is a lapse, not a reason to give up.
Reconsider an agreement that no longer holds before breaking it. “I feel cramped in our agreement, let’s revisit it” is harder to say than any secret, but only it leads out of the circle.

Keep no one else’s lion on one’s own chain. A loved one’s addiction is not karma but a reason to see addiction specialists; relatives have support groups such as Al-Anon. Violence or threats call for real help, not work with numbers.

report: In the worked-through version the person knows passion from the inside, can keep their word and does not fear their own power. They can be trusted with money, power and other people’s secrets — not because they are never tempted, but because they know how temptation pulls and say so out loud. This is the Hierophant at his best: a mentor without hypocrisy. **Faithfulness holds only on what has been chosen, not on what has been hidden.**

Waite ends his description of the Devil with a promise: the one exalted above the chained figures “is not to be their master for ever”. In his deck the same chain appears twice — of iron on the fifteenth card, of flowers on the eighth. The 15-5-8 tail is the path from one to the other. The chain stays. The material changes.
